title: State v. Albaidhani
description: Whether law enforcement officers qualify as "victims" under Marsy's Law and are entitled to have their names redacted from public filings.
plaintiff_argument: Officers One and Two argued that they qualify as victims under Marsy's Law and are entitled to have their names and identifying information redacted from public filings to prevent harassment.
defendant_argument: Samir Albaidhani argued that Marsy's Law does not apply to law enforcement officers and that redacting names would violate his constitutional rights, including the right to confront accusers, and that there is no victim until a conviction.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's decision, holding that law enforcement officers can be victims under Marsy's Law and their names/initials can be redacted from public filings if they could be used to locate or harass them, remanding the case for a balancing test of the victims' rights against the defendant's and public's rights.

title: In re: Lieutenant Governor’s Power to Vote on Final Passage of Legislation
description: Whether the South Dakota Constitution grants the Lieutenant Governor, while serving as President of the Senate, the authority to cast a tie-breaking vote on the final passage of a bill or joint resolution.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor sought an advisory opinion, implying the Lieutenant Governor possesses the constitutional authority to cast a tie-breaking vote on final passage of legislation.
defendant_argument: The Senate Leadership argued that the Lieutenant Governor lacks the authority to cast a tie-breaking vote on final passage of a bill, asserting that only elected members of the Senate should vote on final passage.
decision_outcome: The South Dakota Supreme Court ruled that the state Constitution empowers the Lieutenant Governor, while serving as President of the Senate, to cast a tie-breaking vote in the Senate on any matter, including the final passage of a bill.

title: Gonzales v. Markland
description: Whether the habeas court erred in concluding that the jury district violated Gonzales' right under the South Dakota Constitution to a trial from the "county or district" where the offense was committed and denied her a jury from a fair cross-section of her peers under the Sixth Amendment, with Gonzales arguing these rights were violated and the State arguing they were not.
plaintiff_argument: Gonzales argued that the jury district used for her trial unconstitutionally diluted the percentage of prospective Native American jurors, violating her Sixth Amendment right to a fair cross-section of the community and her right to a trial from the proper "county or district" under the South Dakota Constitution, and that her counsel was ineffective.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the habeas court erred in its interpretation of the United States and South Dakota Constitutions and its application of the Duren test, asserting that the combined jury district was constitutionally valid, represented a fair cross-section of the community, and did not violate the "county or district" requirement.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the habeas court's judgment, finding no constitutional violation in the jury district selection and no deprivation of Gonzales' rights to a fair and impartial jury or effective assistance of counsel.

title: State v. Waldner
description: Whether the circuit court erred by requiring E.H. to produce her diaries and journals, considering E.H.'s constitutional right to privacy under Marsy's Law versus the defendants' right to a fair trial, and whether the subpoena met the requirements of the Nixon factors.
plaintiff_argument: E.H. argued that her right to privacy under Marsy's Law is absolute, that she did not waive this right by disclosing one journal, and that the Waldners' subpoena duces tecum failed to satisfy the three-part Nixon test for relevancy, admissibility, and specificity.
defendant_argument: The Waldners argued that E.H. waived her right to privacy by disclosing one journal and that their constitutional right to a fair trial outweighed E.H.'s privacy rights. They also contended that the journals were relevant to E.H.'s credibility and could be used for impeachment.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's order denying E.H.'s motion to quash the subpoena duces tecum and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: In re Noem
description: Whether Article III, § 12 of the South Dakota Constitution prohibits all contracts between legislators and the State.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor sought an advisory opinion to clarify the application of Article III, § 12, particularly whether a legislator's interest in a state contract, even if indirect, falls under the constitutional prohibition when authorized by a general appropriation bill.
defendant_argument: The Legislature argued that Article III, § 12 only prohibits contracts "authorized" by specific laws passed during a legislator's term, not by general appropriation bills, and requested the court to overrule prior precedent that held otherwise.
decision_outcome: The court overruled its prior decisions in Asphalt Surfacing and Pitts, holding that general appropriation legislation does not, by itself, authorize specific contracts in a way that triggers the prohibition of Article III, § 12.

title: In re: Legislator Interest in State Contracts
description: Whether Article III, § 12 of the South Dakota Constitution prohibits all contracts between legislators and the State, specifically those authorized by general appropriation bills.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor, reflecting existing precedent and concerns among legislators, sought clarity on whether Article III, § 12 broadly prohibits legislators from being interested in any contract with the State, including those funded by general appropriation bills, due to the expansive interpretation of 'authorization'.
defendant_argument: The Legislature argued that general appropriation bills merely allocate funds for ordinary expenses and do not 'authorize' specific contracts in the manner prohibited by Article III, § 12, asserting that prior rulings to the contrary were a misinterpretation of the constitutional text.
decision_outcome: The court overruled its prior decisions in Asphalt Surfacing and Pitts, holding that general appropriation legislation only allocates money to fund state government and does not, by itself, authorize specific contracts relating to ordinary or current expenses, thus narrowing the scope of Article III, § 12's prohibition.

title: Thom v. Barnett (In re Election Contest Dakota Constitution to Legalize)
description: Whether Initiated Constitutional Amendment A, which legalizes, regulates, and taxes marijuana and mandates legislation for medical marijuana and hemp, violates the single-subject rule of the South Dakota Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Amendment A violated Article XXIII, § 1 of the South Dakota Constitution by embracing multiple distinct subjects and was a constitutional revision requiring a convention under Article XXIII, § 2.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Amendment A complied with Article XXIII, § 1 and § 2, as it pertained to no more than one subject and amended rather than revised the Constitution.
decision_outcome: The South Dakota Supreme Court affirmed the circuit court's decision that Initiated Constitutional Amendment A violated the single-subject rule of the South Dakota Constitution and was therefore void in its entirety.

title: Hamen v. Hamlin County
description: Whether damage caused to private property by law enforcement during the arrest of an alleged fleeing felon is a compensable taking under the state constitution, and whether the Sheriff is entitled to qualified immunity for alleged Fourth Amendment violations related to warrantless entry and excessive force.
plaintiff_argument: The Hamens argued that the damage to their mobile home was a compensable taking under the state constitution because law enforcement exceeded its police power, and that the Sheriff violated their Fourth Amendment rights through unlawful warrantless entry and excessive force, for which he should not receive qualified immunity.
defendant_argument: The Sheriff argued that the property damage was an exercise of police power, not a compensable taking for public use, and that he was entitled to qualified immunity for his actions because no constitutional violations occurred or the rights were not clearly established.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's denial of summary judgment on the inverse condemnation claim, dismissing it. It affirmed the denial of summary judgment on the Sheriff's qualified immunity for the unlawful entry claim, remanding it for further proceedings. It reversed the denial of summary judgment on the Sheriff's qualified immunity for the excessive force claim, dismissing it.
